figures.finding: Puerto Rico levies its own income tax on residents: 0% to USD 9,000 of net taxable income, 7% to 25,000, 14% to 41,500, 25% to 61,500 and 33% above, with a 5% gradual adjustment tax above USD 500,000; there is no municipal income tax.
figures.applies: Rates in effect for 2018 and later years, so for 2026; the alternate basic tax is not modelled here.

sources.said: Net taxable income (USD) Tax Not over 9,000 0% Over 9,000, but not over 25,000 7% of the excess over USD 9,000 Over 25,000, but not over 41,500 USD 1,120 plus 14% of the excess over USD 25,000 Over 41,500, but not over 61,500 USD 3,430 plus 25% of the excess over USD 41,500 Over 61,500 USD 8,430 plus 33% of the excess over USD 61,500
This tax is 5% of the excess of the total net taxable income over USD 500,000

figures.finding: The tax year is the calendar year; the return and any balance are due 15 April of the next year (six-month extension on request), with quarterly estimated payments on 15 April, 15 June, 15 September and 15 January.

sources.said: In most cases, taxpayers must file an individual income tax return on a calendar-year basis by 15 April of the following year.
must generally make quarterly payments of estimated tax due 15 April, 15 June, 15 September, and 15 January.

figures.finding: Social security follows the United States: Puerto Rico employers and employees pay US Social Security and Medicare taxes, plus Puerto Rico disability and unemployment payroll taxes.
figures.applies: US FICA rates and wage base are those of the US entry.

sources.said: Puerto Rico is covered under the US social security system; consequently, Puerto Rico employers and employees are subject to the US Social Security and Medicare taxes requirements.
These payroll taxes are: Social Security and Medicare taxes, disability benefits tax, and chauffeur's and other employees' employment security tax.

figures.finding: Employers withhold by Hacienda's tables; a resident paid for services (not as an employee) by another resident has 10% withheld, except on the first USD 500.

sources.said: In the case of a Puerto Rican resident who provides services (rather than as an employee) to another resident person, the income earned while providing such services will be subject to a withholding flat rate of 10%. Such withholding tax (WHT) rate does not apply to the first USD 500 of income earned by the individual who provides the services.

figures.finding: A non-resident is taxed only on Puerto Rico-source income, which includes services performed there; pay to a non-resident has a flat 29% withheld for a foreign national and 20% for a US citizen. Puerto Rico has no tax treaties.

sources.said: Puerto Rican non-residents are only taxed in Puerto Rico on their Puerto Rico-source income.
Puerto Rican employees who are non-residents are subject to a flat 29% withholding in the case of foreign nationals and to a 20% withholding in the case of US citizens.
There are no tax treaties between foreign countries and Puerto Rico.

figures.finding: There is no VAT; sales and use tax (IVU) is 11.5% (10.5% state, 1% municipal), and designated professional and business-to-business services bear 4%; services of merchants with annual business volume under USD 50,000 are excluded (USD 300,000 for services to other merchants).

sources.said: The SUT rate is imposed at 10.5% at the state level and an additional 1% at the municipal level, for an aggregate 11.5%. Designated professional services and business-to-business (B2B) services are taxed at a 4% SUT rate.
Services rendered by merchants with annual volume of business of less than USD 50,000.
Effective 1 July 2020, services to other merchants rendered by merchants with annual volume of business of less than USD 300,000.
